ranked_moves.title: A structure record of the pinned tree: Syzygy derives the repository's shape before anyone writes
ranked_moves.relation: sharpens P9, P10 and the retained parser-derived-structure idea
ranked_moves.prereq: none for slice 1 (tree metadata only); slices 2 and 3 need Q1, because manifests and workflow files are excluded from reading today; a brief clause (spec REQ-034) to hand the record to the author
ranked_moves.what: A deterministic derive stage writes a structure record for the pinned revision in three tiers: path-only facts (sizes, language mix, vendored and generated code set aside, citable versus not citable under the policy); format recognizers (workspace and package manifests, binaries and scripts, CI jobs, compose, Kubernetes and Terraform topology); later, lexical import graphs. Each fact carries its rule, rule version, path and lines, and each rule states its own coverage. A fact states only what its rule matched ('path P matches the vendored-path rule, version 1', 'this manifest declares X'), never an interpretation or runtime behaviour. For a private repository, no size or object-id-derived fact is computed or rendered for a blob the policy excludes or withholds (policy line 89). From the record Syzygy computes a trait profile (has a CLI, a library API, a service, plugins, infrastructure, a data model, a docs site, size class) and, after the run, a coverage map of what the draft cited.
ranked_moves.why: It does four jobs at once: it is the scaffold for figures, the witness for each arrow, the denominator for coverage (the newest run inspected 22 of 1,861 files and nothing said so), and the profile that makes the page plan general. It replaces 'pick one archetype' with computed traits.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] drafts/rev-4.json discovery lists 22 inspected and 12 selected of 1,861 paths at the pinned commit; no Syzygy-side coverage measure exists. [Inferred] that format recognizers cover most public repositories.
slices: S1: path-only record, vendored exclusion and profile basics, printed by check (reads no blob)
S2: recognizers for package.json, Cargo, pyproject, go.mod and GitHub Actions with golden fixtures and a mutation run
S3: compose, Kubernetes, Terraform, Makefile and CMake; the coverage remainder rendered
S4: lexical import scanners collapsed to units

ranked_moves.title: Arrows with receipts: derived facts render as Observed, every relationship is typed and witnessed, every figure prints its evidence tally
ranked_moves.relation: new; sharpens P12's epistemic encoding and P3's ribbon; retires run 3's 'needs an RFC 0007 label amendment' prerequisite
ranked_moves.prereq: an owner answer on the doctrine reading (decision pursuit-2026-11-21-observed-derived); then one dossier spec clause by agent adoption; slice 3 needs Q2 slice 2, which needs Q1
ranked_moves.what: Widen the spec clause that reserves Observed for verified quotations so that it also covers a structural fact Syzygy derived by a declared, versioned, deterministic rule; an agent still never labels anything Observed. Conditions the reading carries: the structure record is an evidence artifact (durable, identified, integrity-verifiable, with source, capture time, scope and provenance); the derived-fact class declares a currency bound, or its claims render Unknown; a figure that mixes derived and authored elements carries machine-readable provenance and never imitates a computed map (RFC7-28); a derived fact states only what its rule matched; and nothing is derived from the size or object id of a blob withheld in a private repository. Staging is the default: tree-metadata facts first, and a recognizer's facts only once it has fixtures and a mutation run (CC-TEST-3, CC-TEST-6). Give every diagram edge a closed relation type. Check upgrades an edge to Observed only when the structure record holds a fact of the identical relation type between the same two units (an authored 'calls' is not witnessed by a manifest's 'declares a dependency'), and raises a finding when coverage was complete and no witness exists. Generate each figure's legend from the encodings it actually uses, and print a computed tally under each figure ('14 relationships: 9 derived by Syzygy, 5 cited readings, 0 unsupported').

units.gap: The integrity core is repository-agnostic, but what the mechanism lets an author read and cite, and what it asks the author to write, are shaped by Butlers and by servers. The sharpest limit is new to this pursuit: the content-classification policy every dossier run uses is the Butlers project-shape policy (policyId 'polaris-butlers-project-shape-secrets'). It admits as citable only one-segment root documents with 16 fixed stems, Markdown/RST/TXT under a top-level docs/ or doc/, licences, two governance-text names, and code in 25 extensions. It refuses as project documentation any docs path containing 'architecture', 'design', 'adr', 'decision', 'rfc' or 'spec': exactly the files a manifesto most needs for diagrams and choices. It cannot cite YAML, TOML, JSON, HCL/Terraform, Dockerfiles, Makefiles, CMake, protobuf, notebooks, MDX/AsciiDoc docs sites, Vue/Svelte, Scala, Elixir, Haskell, Dart or Zig, nor a package README below the root of a monorepo. A claim citing only such files renders Unknown or withheld. On top of that the brief fixes four reader topics built around 'end-to-end workflows' and 'mechanisms', a seven-dimension technology table written for networked servers (networking, concurrency, persistence), example sentences about replicas and caches, at most three deep dives and a flat exploration with no partition: the newest run cited from 22 of Redis's 1,861 files (1.2%). What is already general and worth protecting: Git-object citation and quote verification for any text, Poles chosen from what the repository holds ('never fill a fixed template'), a per-run declared audience (landed after the newest run), why-first with an Unknown fallback, and the schema's presentation elements. Every claim about non-Redis behaviour here is Inferred: all six runs on disk are redis/redis, and the only shaped test fixture is a synthetic Redis-like tree.

findings.claim: The dossier's citable set is defined by a Butlers-derived policy that excludes, as project documentation, every docs path whose directory or file name contains architecture, design, adr, decision, rfc, spec, governance or principle, and admits docs only under top-level docs/ or doc/ in .md/.rst/.txt. Architecture and design docs, the best source for a manifesto's diagrams and choices, cannot be cited in any repository.

units.gap: Readability today comes from careful writing rules, not from structure or measurement. The brief's voice and readability rules (category term first, flat facts, short sentences, lists as elements, 300-word sections, few deep dives) and 25 reader standards produce clear, plain sentences, and they work: median sentence 15-20 words on the reading pages. But the page model gives a reader almost no structure to scan: every Pole is one H2 section with no H3 anywhere on the reading path (0 H3 across 5 pages), so a 750-word page has one heading; citations dominate the links (31-70 citation links per page against 2-4 navigation links); the fixed apparatus (draft banner, provenance sentence, six-item legend, 61-word review status) is about 200 words on every reading page, 47% of all the text on 'Serving a command'. What enforces readability is four counters (RS-13 titles, RS-14 deep-dive count, RS-16 sections with no diagram, RS-19 section words) that are advice on the check's report, never stored, and a design reviewer who reads HTML source: it passed every reading page 'acceptable' while one diagram overflowed by 1,267px and every page scrolled sideways on a phone, with 0 mentions of overflow, scroll, mobile or width across its 27 findings. It also kept raising advisories the author cannot fix (a figure for the deep dive, line numbers on source pages), so 'ready' already means 'ready except what the mechanism cannot do'. An 'extremely readable' bar would need what nothing asks for or measures today: a page outline (H3s) and a skim path, a measured first screen, apparatus off the reading path, progressive disclosure tied to reader intent, term popovers, a reading-time and density budget per page type, and a comprehension test.

Generality is bounded first by what may be cited: the Butlers-derived classification policy excludes architecture, design, ADR, RFC and spec documents and most config/IaC/notebook formats. Visual richness is bounded by a single layered graph whose 'kind' is a label, by deep dives that cannot hold a figure, and by a wrap rule that fails on the commonest flow shape. Readability is bounded by a flat section model with no subsections and by gates that never see pixels. The highest-value moves are therefore enabling changes: a dossier-own source policy, typed figure records attachable to any page, a subsection outline, and stored measurements. They sit under run 3's P3, P5, P9, P10 and P12 rather than replacing them, and they should land before the generality probe (fnry.22) so that the probe measures the mechanism rather than the Butlers policy.

units.gap: The mechanism can draw exactly one picture: a node-and-edge graph laid out in layers left to right, whatever its declared kind. The six kinds (flow, lifecycle, state-machine, boundary, dependency, placement) are a label: diagram-layout.ts never reads `kind`, and the renderer prints it as a reader-visible eyebrow. There is no grouping or containment, no lanes, no time axis, no ordered messages, no node shapes beyond a 200x56 rectangle, no per-node emphasis, no annotation, no legend beyond line style, no image, no link from a node, and no layout that wraps anything but a plain chain (so the commonest real flow, a chain that fans out at the end, renders as one unbounded row). Deep dives cannot carry a diagram at all: a diagram must name a section, and the one call site that draws figures is the section loop. The renderer's strengths are real and worth keeping: deterministic layout, careful label placement with leader lines, an inert-SVG allow-list, a full text list of every node and edge with its citations and marking, Pole hues and dark mode. The code excerpt is the richest 'show' form the schema has (Syzygy renders 1-60 cited lines from its own read and marks them Observed), yet it has been used 0 times in every stored draft, has no line numbers or highlight, and cannot be annotated. Nothing checks that a diagram is true to the source beyond per-element citations and the fidelity reviewer's per-element reading; nothing checks that it is the right picture, fits its column, or is not a list in disguise.

units.framing: Generality is a property of the mechanism, not of the prompt. Today the mechanism has one shape baked in. The brief fixes four topics in a fixed order (brief.ts:47-52), a seven-dimension technology table, one diagram layout, and a Pole rule that relies on the agent's judgement. Every live run has been redis/redis. Run 3's P9 proposed an archetype fingerprint that selects packs. This lens argues for a different primitive: traits, not archetypes. Real repositories are combinations (a CLI that is also a library, a server with a plugin SDK, a monorepo of all three). A trait vector computed deterministically from the pinned tree composes page-plan modules additively, and a new shape should cost a data file and a fixture, not code. It also covers budget scaling from 2k to 5M lines, what to do when no thesis is stated anywhere, and how to prove generality continuously without paying for LLM runs on every change.

findings.claim: Shapes that neither run 3 nor TARGETS.md names, and what each would break today. Framework (the 'user' is a developer extending it, so the key figure is the extension-point lifecycle and the brief's 'end-to-end workflow' topic misleads). Infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, Helm or Kustomize: the architecture is in the declarations, and a derived resource graph is nearly the whole answer). Data or ML research code (notebooks, configs, a training pipeline: the thesis lives in a paper or README and the 'workflow' is a pipeline DAG). Mobile app (platform manifests and screen or navigation graph; build variants). Firmware or embedded (linker scripts, a board or hardware abstraction layer, interrupt-driven state machines; C with no package manifest). Docs-only or spec-only (the repository is the product: the IA is the architecture). Plugin ecosystem (core plus N plugins following one contract: small multiples of one plugin shape). Polyglot monorepo with hundreds of packages (the unit graph is the map; no single thesis). Almost-no-docs repo (the thesis must be marked as inferred from code). Docs-elsewhere repo (README links to an external site the run may not fetch). Each of these trips at least one fixed assumption: the four fixed topics, the server-shaped technology table, the single layout, or a thesis that is always stated somewhere.

moves.title: Repository profile as a trait vector, computed before authoring
moves.what: Extend I1-M1's derived record with a `profile`. Each field is a deterministic trait with its evidence path. Fields: languages by first-party bytes (vendored and generated excluded by linguist-style rules plus the repo's .gitattributes, I3-F2); size class (by first-party bytes: XS under 100 KB, S, M, L, XL over 50 MB); layout (single-unit, workspace with N units, polyglot with N units in K ecosystems, docs-dominant); surfaces present (binary targets → `has-cli`; library exports or published-package metadata → `has-library-api`; server entry signatures in manifests or Dockerfile EXPOSE → `has-service`; plugin contract (a directory of siblings sharing one manifest shape) → `has-plugins`; IaC files → `has-infrastructure`; notebooks or ML configs → `has-pipeline`; linker scripts or board files → `has-firmware`; schema or migrations → `has-data-model`); documentation (README length and heading tree, a docs-site config with its nav (mkdocs.yml nav, docusaurus sidebars, Sphinx toctree, mdBook SUMMARY.md), ADR directory, examples directory, external docs links found in README, recorded as link targets that were not fetched); tests (frameworks by config file, test-to-source byte ratio); CI (workflows and jobs from I1-M1); licence (SPDX id by exact-text match of the LICENSE file against the SPDX list, or Unknown). The author never edits the profile. The draft may add `understanding.shape`, an Inferred, cited reading of what the traits mean together.
moves.why: Run 3's P9 picks one archetype from a closed list. Real repos are mixtures, and a misclassified archetype silently shapes the whole dossier. Traits compose, and each trait has a mechanical witness, so the profile is Observed rather than a guess.
moves.truth_preservation: Each trait carries its witness paths and rule id. A trait whose witness rule did not run, or whose input screening withheld, is Unknown, never false. The profile renders on the review report as Syzygy's observation, separate from the agent's `shape` reading.
moves.generalization: This is the generality mechanism itself: plans key on traits, so an unseen combination still gets every module its traits imply.
integration_points: dossier-site.ts review report: a 'What Syzygy measured' block

moves.title: Shape packs as data: a new repository shape costs a JSON file and a fixture, not code
moves.what: Shape packs live in a versioned directory, `polaris-shape-packs/<trait>.json`. Each pack has five parts. (a) Trigger: the trait it attaches to. (b) Recognizers: declarative extractors for that shape's self-description formats, written as path glob plus format (json, toml or yaml) plus a field mapping to a derived-table schema. Redis's src/commands/*.json maps to a `commands` table with columns from `$.*.arity`, `$.*.group` and `$.*.since` (illustrative paths) with no code. (c) Page-plan modules: pages or sections to add (for example, has-cli adds 'The command surface' with a required `matrix` or derived table, has-plugins adds 'Anatomy of a plugin' with small multiples, has-infrastructure adds 'What gets deployed where' with a containment figure built from the derived resource graph). (d) A question pack: the reader questions that module must answer. (e) Glossary seeds and the technology-table dimensions that apply. The brief or plan composes the modules of all present traits, de-duplicates them, and orders them by a fixed module precedence. Packs are hashed into the run record and the brief names their versions.
moves.why: The owner wants any codebase. Shapes are open-ended, so the extension point must not be code. It also separates the two things P9 bundled: detecting a shape (deterministic, I3-M1) and what to do about it (editorial policy, here data that can be reviewed and A/B'd per corpus run).
moves.truth_preservation: A recognizer's output is derived and Observed under I1-M2 only if its mapping is deterministic and its target paths resolve. A pack can request content but never assert it: a requested section the evidence cannot fill is an `unresolved` disposition, as today. Pack versions are recorded per run, so a dossier can be re-explained ('this page exists because trait has-cli was witnessed by Cargo.toml [[bin]]').
moves.generalization: This is the minimum mechanism for a new shape without new code: one pack file, plus one synthetic fixture for I3-M5. Recognizer formats are bounded (json, toml, yaml, line-oriented). Anything needing a real parser stays T3 and is out of pack scope.

moves.title: A scale ladder: exploration strategy, partition and page plan as functions of measured size
moves.what: From the profile's first-party bytes and unit count, Syzygy picks one of four exploration tiers and states it in the run record. XS/S (single unit, under about 2 MB): one session; target coverage is every first-party file inspected; deep dives at most 2. M (a few units or 2-20 MB): partition by manifest units, or else by directory, splitting until each part is at most 1 MB of first-party code; one scout pass per part (P10). L (20-200 MB or more than 20 units): partition as M, then rank parts by a deterministic centrality score (in-degree in the derived unit or import graph, plus docs mentions, plus entry-point ownership); deep-scout the top K for the budget; the remainder get derived-only cards (name, path, size, derived edges, Observed) and are marked `deferred-by-budget` for prose. XL (5M lines and up): as L, plus small-multiple atlas pages per top-level domain. The landing thesis is built from the domain level, never from a leaf. The coverage map renders three bands per part: deep-read, derived-only, and withheld or unparsed. The denominator is first-party bytes, so 'covered' means something.
moves.why: Run 3's P10 named partition plus scouts plus coverage but no partition algorithm, no ranking, and no notion of a derived-only card. Derived-only cards are what make a 300-package monorepo honest at bounded cost: every package appears with Observed facts, and only the important ones get prose.
moves.truth_preservation: The coverage map is computed from derived bytes and the draft's cards. A derived-only card asserts only derived facts. Deferred parts are visible, never silently absent (VIS-2). The centrality score is deterministic and stated, so 'why these 12 packages got prose' is answerable.
moves.generalization: Size-driven and format-keyed, so it holds from a 2k-line CLI to a 5M-line monorepo. The thresholds are parameters for the corpus (I3-M5) to tune.

moves.title: When nobody states the thesis: an explicitly code-inferred thesis, and external docs named but not read
moves.what: There are three thesis states, each rendered differently. (1) Stated: the thesis cites a maintainer statement of purpose (README, docs, package description field, which is derived). (2) Code-inferred: no source states purpose, so the author may write a thesis marked `basis: code-reading`. It must cite at least two entry points or public surfaces, and it renders under a visible tag: 'No maintainer statement of purpose was found; this summary is Polaris's reading of the code.' (3) Unknown: neither exists. For docs-elsewhere repos, the derived README link targets (I3-M1) are listed in a 'Documentation that lives elsewhere (not read)' line, the external content is Unknown, and the run record states the egress boundary. `check` enforces two things. A stated thesis must cite a file whose path or derived role is documentation or package metadata. A code-inferred thesis must not use maintainer-voice verbs ('is designed to', 'aims to'); this is a lexical advisory, since intent is not readable from code.
moves.why: TARGETS.md asks exactly this ('does the generator invent a thesis where none is stated, or say Unknown?'). The current answer is the BRIEF_TOPICS rule 'an unknown block here, never an invented reason' (brief.ts:48). That rule is honest but leaves the landing page empty for a large class of repos, which is not readable. A labelled reading of the code is both true (as Inferred) and useful.
moves.truth_preservation: Intent is never inferred: the code-inferred thesis states what the code does, not why it was made. The tag is Syzygy-rendered from the `basis` field, not author prose. External docs are named as Observed link targets with Unknown content. Nothing is fetched (no egress change).
moves.generalization: It applies to every thin-docs repo, which is most research code, most firmware and many internal tools.
integration_points: brief.ts BRIEF_TOPICS[0] text plus the voice rules

moves.title: Shape matrix: synthetic fixtures prove the mechanism on every commit; a small live corpus proves the writing
moves.what: There are two tiers. Tier A runs with no LLM in CI on every change. Synthetic git repos are generated by script into test fixtures: a Rust CLI with 2 crates; a 300-package TypeScript workspace with a generated dependency graph; a Python library plus docs site; Terraform with modules; a notebook pipeline; C firmware with a linker script; a docs-only repo; a plugin host with 12 plugins; a no-README repo. Each runs derive, profile, page plan and render against a canned draft generated from the derived record alone (derived-only cards, hero from the base graph). Each asserts its shape's acceptance properties: the expected traits fire, the required modules appear, no horizontal scroll at 390 px (P6 probe), figure node counts stay within the readable bound, and the coverage map's denominators are exact. Tier B is live, periodic and owner-scheduled: three to five real public repos (fnry.22's requests, ripgrep and vite, plus one IaC and one thin-docs repo) with frozen per-shape acceptance questions, scored by the P7 probe and stored as a scorecard per mechanism version.
moves.why: L8: one repository measures nothing about generality. Live runs are expensive and rare, so most generality regressions (a trait that stops firing, a layout that overflows on a 300-node graph) are mechanical and should be caught for free. Tier A makes 'works on X' an Observed claim about the mechanism, leaving only the writing quality as Inferred.
moves.truth_preservation: Tier A claims only mechanical properties, and its fixtures are inputs with literal expected values (the repo's conformance discipline). Tier B scores stay advice and are never a readiness oracle. Each score names the mechanism version and fixture digest (rule 11).
moves.generalization: Adding a shape means adding a pack (I3-M2) and a fixture generator. The matrix grows with the packs.

units.framing: Today every structural picture in a dossier is drawn by the authoring agent from what it chose to read, and every element of it is Inferred. In the newest Redis run the agent cited 20 distinct paths of a 1,861-blob tree and drew three hand-made boxes-and-arrows diagrams, while machine-readable structure that Syzygy could have derived deterministically (manifests, 11 CI workflows, 459 command-definition files, the directory/size shape) went unused. The lens asks: what can Syzygy compute itself from the pinned tree, how should it be labelled under doctrine as written, and how does the author use it as a scaffold to edit rather than a picture to redraw. The central finding is that doctrine already has room for this: trust-and-evidence.md defines Observed as 'a deterministic claim with a resolvable evidence link', and RFC7-28 already distinguishes curated from computed visuals. What reserves Observed for verified quotations is a dossier spec clause, which since D10 is agent-decidable. Run 3 parked this as needing a label amendment; that was too pessimistic.

findings.claim: The newest Redis draft (rev-4) cites 20 distinct paths out of 1,861 blobs. 78 citations go to redis.conf, 63 to README.md and 31 to MANIFESTO. No citation lands under tests/ (129 unit-test paths, 4.4 MB), .github/workflows/ (11 workflow files), deps/ (6.2 MB of vendored code), or src/commands/ (459 JSON command definitions). The agent's own stopping reason is: 'Every reader question was answered from README, MANIFESTO, redis.conf and the request path in src'. The agent self-reports 22 inspected paths.

findings.claim: Doctrine already lets a deterministic, derived structural fact be Observed. trust-and-evidence.md:105 says 'Observed — a deterministic claim with a resolvable evidence link'. RFC7-28 already says 'curated/computed provenance is a machine-readable attribute on every visual' and 'embedded computed visuals inherit the map surface's obligations'. What reserves Observed for verified quotations is the dossier spec: polaris-dossier-local-agent-mode spec.md:236 says 'Observed is reserved for a quotation that Syzygy has verified'. Run 3's I3-M2 said rendering derived structure as Observed 'needs an RFC7 epistemic-label amendment'. Read against these clauses it needs neither a doctrine nor an RFC amendment, only a spec amendment, which D10 made agent-decidable.

findings.claim: Cost tiers for derived structure, from cheapest to most expensive. T0, path-only (tree listing and sizes): directory treemap, language mix by extension and bytes, presence and size of docs, tests, CI, examples and vendored code, and the manifest inventory. This is language-agnostic, reads no blob and is already within what census.ts does. T1, format recognizers over screened manifest blobs, using one grammar per file format, never per programming language: package.json, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, go.mod, pom.xml, *.csproj, CMakeLists add_executable/add_library, Makefile target lines, GitHub, GitLab and CircleCI workflow YAML (jobs, needs, triggers), docker-compose (services, depends_on, ports), Dockerfile (FROM, EXPOSE, ENTRYPOINT), Helm Chart.yaml and Kubernetes kinds, Terraform blocks, OpenAPI, .proto, GraphQL SDL, SQL DDL, Prisma, JSON Schema. These give the workspace/package graph, binaries, scripts, the CI pipeline graph, service topology, API and route tables, and data models. T2, lexical import scanners per language (import/require/use/mod/#include lines), about 50-150 lines each for the top 10 languages: a file- and package-level import graph, true at the lexical level. T3, tree-sitter or LSP-class symbol and call indexes: public API surface, call graphs. These need native or WASM grammars, the runtime and supply-chain cost that brings, and per-language maintenance. Most of the visual value sits in T0+T1, about 80% by this lane's judgement.
findings.label: Inferred
findings.basis: Design judgement. Supporting observation: on Redis, T0 alone separates src/deps/tests/modules (I1-F1). T1 Makefile and workflow parsing would give the build/CI graph, and recognising the 459 command JSONs (a project-specific self-description format) would give the full command table. The generality of T1 across repos is unmeasured (all six runs are of redis/redis).

moves.title: Pinned-tree structure record: Syzygy derives the repository's shape before anyone writes
moves.what: A new deterministic stage, `syzygy dossier derive`, runs after init and before the brief. It writes `derived/structure.json`, frozen and digest-bound like the draft schema. The record holds: (a) T0 tree facts (directory tree with byte and file counts, language mix, docs/tests/CI/examples/vendored flags, largest subtrees); (b) T1 manifest units, meaning each package, crate, module or workspace member with its path, its declared name, its binaries and scripts, and its declared dependencies on other in-repo units (an edge list); (c) a CI pipeline graph (workflow → job → needs edges, triggers); (d) a service topology when compose or Kubernetes files exist; (e) the T2 lexical import graph collapsed to unit level, once the scanners exist. Every fact carries `{rule, ruleVersion, path, startLine, endLine}`, so each node and edge resolves to the bytes that state it. Every record also carries its own coverage: the files each rule considered, parsed, could not parse, and that screening withheld.
moves.why: It makes structure Syzygy's observation rather than the agent's guess (VIS-1, truth first). It turns 'what is in this repo' from an exploration problem into a lookup, so the author's budget goes to argument. It is the input every later move needs: archetype detection (P9), subsystem partition (P10), derived diagrams (I1-M3), the generality profile (lens 3).
moves.truth_preservation: Derived facts are claims at the resolution of the rule, never above it. 'Cargo.toml at lines 12-14 declares a dependency on crate core' is true by construction. 'crate cli calls core at runtime' is never derived. Each rule has golden fixtures and a rule-6 mutation run, and a rule that cannot parse a file records `unparsed` (Unknown), never 'no edges' (VIS-2). The coverage block renders as a remainder: '38 of 41 manifests parsed; 3 Unknown (unsupported format)'. The record is deterministic and re-runnable from the pinned commit, which is what RFC7-28 asks of a computed visual.
moves.generalization: This is the most general mechanism available, because it keys on file formats rather than on project archetypes or programming languages. A repository using a format with no rule still gets T0 and an honest Unknown for the rest. New formats are data-driven recognizer entries; see lens 3.

moves.title: Derived is Observed, by derivation: the label answer that needs no doctrine change
moves.what: Widen the dossier spec's label clause from 'Observed is reserved for a quotation that Syzygy has verified' to 'Observed is reserved for what Syzygy itself establishes from the pinned tree: a quotation it verified, or a structural fact it derived by a declared, versioned, deterministic rule, rendered with that rule's provenance'. An agent still never labels anything Observed. The renderer shows a derived element with the Observed line style. Its evidence pop says 'Derived by Syzygy: `cargo-workspace@1` from Cargo.toml, lines 12–14' instead of a quotation. Every visual carries the RFC7-28 machine attribute `data-provenance="computed|curated|mixed"`. Two fallbacks remain if a reviewer rejects that reading of 'deterministic'. B: a fourth presentation mark, 'Derived', glossed in the legend as 'computed by Syzygy from the files, at the stated rule's resolution'. Because it is an encoding, not a new epistemic label, it is still Observed underneath (VIS-7 is satisfied by the legend). C, which needs zero spec change: render derived elements Inferred, with provenance naming the rule. This understates the evidence, but nothing becomes false.
moves.why: It gets the most truthful visual (a box the reader can trust because a machine found it) without a doctrine act, and it corrects run 3's I3-M2 prerequisite. It also restores something the encoding lost: today the legend offers 'Solid: observed', yet the schema's diagram `epistemic` is `inferred|unknown` only (draft-schema.ts:113), so the agent can never draw a solid line. Derived elements would give the solid line a population.
moves.truth_preservation: Three guards. (1) Rule resolution: a rule's claim template is fixed text ('declares a dependency on', 'imports', 'defines job … that needs …'), never semantic paraphrase. (2) Determinism: re-running derive at the pinned commit must give byte-identical output, and `check` re-derives the record and refuses a mismatched digest. (3) Identity: a derived node's id is `path:` or `unit:` plus the canonical name, so the author cannot relabel a derived node into something else. Author relabels are display aliases, shown as 'core (crate `foo-core`)'.
moves.generalization: Format-keyed, as in I1-M1; nothing about the label depends on the project.

moves.title: Scaffold, then annotate: derived views the author edits instead of redraws
moves.what: Syzygy offers each derived graph as a numbered candidate view: unit dependency graph, CI pipeline, service topology, directory map. A draft diagram may declare `base: {view: 'units', digest}` and then only edit. It can group nodes into named clusters (`groups: [{id,label,members}]`), prune nodes with a reason (`hidden: [{id, reason}]`), rename them for display (`alias`), add cited Inferred runtime edges the derivation cannot see (dashed), and annotate a node or edge with a cited one-line note. `check` enforces four things. Every base node is shown, grouped or hidden with a reason. Hidden counts are disclosed on the figure ('showing 9 of 31 packages · full map'). An author edge never duplicates a derived edge. The renderer links 'full map' to an exhaustive computed page.
moves.why: This turns the author's diagram work from drafting (error-prone, and the reason every Redis diagram is a hand-made chain) into editing and explaining, where an LLM is strongest. It also gives the figure a denominator: a reader can see what was left out, which no hand-drawn diagram can say (VIS-2).
moves.truth_preservation: Mixed provenance is visible per element: solid derived, dashed authored, dotted unknown. The figure's `data-provenance` is `mixed`. Pruning is never silent, because the hidden-count chip is Syzygy-rendered, not author-written. A grouping is presentation, not a claim, unless its label asserts something; group labels are presentation labels under the existing 120-character rule.
moves.generalization: Works for any repo with at least one recognised manifest or workflow. A repo with none gets the T0 directory map as its base, so even a single-file research repo has one honest structural figure.
integration_points: check-derive.ts: base coverage and duplicate-edge findings

moves.title: Self-description harvest: turn a repo's own machine-readable tables into reference pages
moves.what: Many repositories ship machine-readable self-descriptions that are better than prose: Redis's 459 src/commands/*.json command specs, OpenAPI documents, .proto services, GraphQL SDL, SQL migrations, Prisma or ORM schema files, JSON Schema, Terraform variables and outputs, Helm values.yaml, CLI definitions in declarative form (a clap derive is parser territory; a cobra or argparse call is not reliably derivable, so those are out). Syzygy recognises them by format (T1) and emits derived tables: commands (name, arity, flags, since-version, group), routes (method, path, operation), entities (fields, types, relations, rendered as an ER figure), config keys (key, default, description where the file carries one). Each becomes an exhaustive, sortable reference page under 'Reference', and the author cites rows (`derivedRow`) rather than re-typing them.
moves.why: L7 says a catalogue is not a manifesto, and that stays true: these pages are the evidence layer one step away, so the argument pages can say 'Redis has about 240 commands in 15 groups' (a derived count, Observed) and link the table. Today the Redis draft's command knowledge comes from README prose (I1-F1), and its config knowledge comes from 78 citations into a 55-screen redis.conf the reader must scroll.
moves.truth_preservation: Rows are derived, not authored, so they are Observed with rule provenance. Counts are computed. A format the recognizer half-understands yields Unknown cells, never guessed ones. Excluded or withheld files are named in the table's coverage line.
moves.generalization: Format-keyed. A project-specific format (Redis's command JSON) is handled by the lens-3 declarative recognizer (I3-M2): a JSON-path mapping file, not code. The generality claim is Inferred until the standing corpus (lens 3) shows two or more shapes.

units.framing: Readability for a newcomer has a small number of mechanical causes. Never meet a word before it is explained. Always know what you can stop reading. Have one concrete thing to hold on to across pages. Have a limit attached to every comparison. The Polaris mechanism already has most of the raw material: an abstraction-tree schema (a parent summarises its children), a glossary surface-form matcher in the renderer, cited understanding items for terminology, and a reader-test engine. What it lacks is the bindings that let `check` see readability: which block defines which term, which depth a block belongs to, which concrete example threads the pages. This lens proposes those bindings and sorts every readability technique by how it can be enforced: mechanically by `check`, by a reader-model probe, or by author guidance only.

findings.claim: The renderer already finds glossary terms in agent prose by surface form: the term, its de-hyphenated form, plural, capitalised and upper-case. It links the first use in each section to its entry with a hover or focus pop-up. It does not know where a term is defined in reading order, so a page can use a term three sections before the prose that explains it, and nothing notices.

findings.claim: Enforceability sort of the readability techniques. Mechanically checkable once the schema carries the binding: definition-before-use in reading order (I4-M1); per-depth word and reading-time budgets (I4-M2); running-example presence on each Pole, with a citation to an example, test or doc file (I4-M3); analogy completeness, meaning every analogy states where it breaks, cited (I4-M4); page-template conformance (answer first, figure, walk, trade-off, next); question-led headings (lexical: interrogative opener or 'How/Why/What' form, advisory); sentence-length and undefined-term density per paragraph. Needs a reader-model probe (P7): whether depth 1 alone answers purpose and thesis; whether the running example clarifies; whether an analogy misleads; whether a figure answers its question (I2-M5). Author guidance only: voice, choice of example, aptness of an analogy, what to put first.

moves.title: Concept graph with define-before-use in reading order
moves.what: The glossary becomes a graph. Each `terminology` understanding item gains `display` (the term as a reader writes it, which fnry.18 also wants), `aliases`, `dependsOn: [termIds]` (terms its definition uses), and `homeBlock` (the block id in the reading path whose text explains it). Syzygy computes the reading order (landing, then Poles in order, then deep dives in link order) and runs the renderer's existing surface-form matcher over every block in that order. Three advisories, each naming the block and term: a term used before its home block; a home block whose own text uses a `dependsOn` term not yet introduced; and a cycle in `dependsOn`. The renderer marks the home block's first occurrence with `<dfn>`, and any earlier occurrence (if the author keeps one) gets the pop-up, so readability degrades gracefully. The glossary page renders the terms in topological order of `dependsOn`, so the glossary itself can be read top to bottom as a primer, with an optional small concept-map figure (containment or graph kind) of the top terms.
moves.why: The single most common newcomer failure is meeting jargon cold. RS-2 ('define each term at first use') is judged by a reviewer today, and the reviewer reads 3.4 MB of HTML. Order is a computable property of the dossier, so computing it is cheaper and more reliable than judging it.
moves.truth_preservation: Definitions stay cited understanding items. `dependsOn` and `homeBlock` are presentation bindings, not claims. The check is deterministic text matching over agent prose only. Quotations and source pages are excluded, as the existing matcher already excludes them.
moves.generalization: Language- and project-neutral. Term forms are the project's own vocabulary.

moves.title: Three reading depths from one tree, switchable without script, each with its own budget and probe
moves.what: Make depth explicit and computed rather than a separate 'skim view'. Depth 1, about 30 seconds: the thesis, the hero figure, and each Pole's one-sentence answer, its first block. Depth 2, about 5 minutes: every section's parent blocks plus figures plus walks (I2-M3). Depth 3: everything, including children, details, deep dives and reference. A block's depth is its tree level, which the schema already encodes, so there is no new authoring burden. The renderer emits `data-depth` on every block and a CSS-only depth switch (three radio inputs, `body:has(#depth-1:checked) [data-depth="2"],[data-depth="3"] {display:none}`). It degrades to everything shown when CSS is off, and it never hides an Unknown that changes a parent's meaning: Unknown-bearing children are promoted to their parent's depth, P3/P4's 'show how many Unknowns a view hides' requirement. `check` computes words and estimated reading time per depth and advises over budget (depth 1 at most 150 words, depth 2 at most 1,500, both tunable from P6 measurements). The P7 comprehension probe runs per depth: the depth-1 view must let a fresh reader state purpose, beneficiary and thesis; the depth-2 view must answer all seven frozen questions.
moves.why: This turns run 3's P4 'skim view' into a measurable layered-reading contract that makes RS-3 to RS-5 (abstraction tree) testable end to end. It gives the owner's 'extremely readable' a number per depth, rather than one global word count.
moves.truth_preservation: Hiding is presentation only, and the Unknown promotion rule keeps every material qualification visible at the depth of the claim it qualifies (AUTHORING.md: 'Never remove a material qualification'). A probe score is advice, never readiness by itself.
moves.generalization: It works for any dossier, because depth derives from the tree. The budgets scale by the I3-M3 size tier.

moves.title: One running example, grounded in the project's own tests and examples, threaded through every Pole as a guided tour
moves.what: The draft names one `example`: a concrete scenario a newcomer can picture ('a client runs SET user:42 Ada, then the server restarts'). Its premise must cite an example, test or documentation file. The derived role from I3-M1 says which files are tests or examples, and tests are the most reliable concrete specifications any repository carries. Each Pole then carries an `exampleStep`: a short block showing what happens to the example at this layer, cited, optionally bound to figure elements through a walk (I2-M3). The renderer shows a slim ribbon on each page ('Following: SET user:42, step 3 of 5: the write reaches the AOF'), with previous and next links that form a guided tour across pages, alongside the sidebar order. `check` enforces two things: the example premise cites a test, example or doc path (advisory if the derived role is unavailable), and each Pole has a step or a `notApplicable` reason.
moves.why: Follow-one-request tours are the most effective device in high-quality hand-made architecture explainers. A single example keeps abstractions anchored and gives the reader continuity between pages that are otherwise separate. Using tests makes the example verifiable, not illustrative.
moves.truth_preservation: Every step is a cited claim. The premise is drawn from the repository's own example or test, so the values in it (keys, commands, file names) appear in a cited source, and a quotation can show them verbatim. The ribbon is Syzygy-rendered navigation. An invented scenario not traceable to a source is prevented by the citation requirement on the premise.
moves.generalization: Every shape has a natural example: a request (server), an invocation (CLI), a call sequence (library), a deploy (IaC), a training run (ML), a boot or interrupt (firmware), a reader's question (docs-only). Shape packs (I3-M2) can suggest the example form per trait.

dossier-site.ts: the example ribbon plus tour links
brief.ts DOSSIER_GUIDANCE: choose the example from tests or examples

S2: premise citation-role check using I3-M1 test and example roles.

moves.title: Analogies with stated limits as a first-class element
moves.what: A new element: `analogy: {id, likeWhat: presentationLabel, framing: non-normative block, breaksWhere: claim block (cited)}`. It renders as a compact aside ('Think of it like a … — Where the analogy breaks: …'). The `framing` part is RFC7-2 (b) non-normative ('framing, motivation, analogy'), so it needs no citation and makes no project claim. The `breaksWhere` part asserts a fact about the project and is cited. `check` refuses an analogy without `breaksWhere` and advises at most one analogy per page.
moves.why: Analogies are the cheapest comprehension accelerator for a newcomer and the most common way explanatory prose smuggles in falsehoods. Making the limit mandatory and cited turns the risk into a feature: the reader learns the project's distinctive property exactly where the analogy fails.
moves.truth_preservation: It uses an existing contract category: RFC7-2 (b) names 'analogy' as explicitly non-normative. The project-fact half is a cited claim like any other.
moves.generalization: Project-neutral.

moves.title: Page templates per page type: answer, figure, walk, cost, next

Deep dive: question title, answer, figure, mechanism walk, cost, back-link to parent element. Reference page (derived): coverage line, table or map, 'cited from' backlinks. Missing slots render nothing. They are never placeholder text, except an Unknown that is material.
moves.why: Consistency is a large part of readability: a reader learns where things are once. A template also removes a whole class of author decisions (ordering), which is where LLM drafts vary most between runs.
moves.truth_preservation: Pure composition. 'Related' links are computed from the draft's own bindings, so they never assert a relationship the sources do not state; the label is 'Shares terms with', not 'Depends on'.
moves.generalization: Page types are project-neutral. Shape packs add page types, not templates per project.

units.framing: Two families do this job. Auto-wiki generators (DeepWiki-style open-source tools, academic CodeWiki, diagram-first GitDiagram-style tools, commercial wikis refreshed in CI) are fast and broad: a page per module, Mermaid diagrams, chat. The research on them reports the same weaknesses: hallucinated or wrong relationships, granularity mismatch (code-level detail in architecture views), and evaluation that leans on LLM judges. Hand-made traditions (C4 and Structurizr's model-based diagrams, arc42 and 4+1 views, Diátaxis, ADRs, literate and annotated source, guided code tours, high-end explorable explanations) are slow but get structure right: one model with many consistent views, a fixed set of viewpoints, a clean split between explanation and reference, decisions recorded as decisions. Polaris already beats the auto-wikis on truth: pinned revisions, mechanically checked citations and quotations, independent review. The adoptable patterns are the hand-made traditions' structural disciplines, made mechanical, plus making the truth advantage visible on the page, where the competition cannot follow. Web queries were generic; only search-result summaries were read, not full papers, so every external claim is Inferred.

findings.claim: Current auto-wiki generators converge on a page per module or subsystem, Mermaid architecture and data-flow diagrams, and an 'ask' or chat feature. One diagram-first tool links diagram components to the real files. One commercial tool refreshes the wiki in CI on every push.

Features not verified against the tools.

findings.claim: The research on LLM-generated architecture documentation reports three recurring defects: hallucinated elements and incorrect relationships; granularity mismatch, with views drawn at code level rather than architectural abstraction; and incomplete or misleading diagrams. Evaluation is mostly LLM-as-judge plus human review. CodeWikiBench builds hierarchical rubrics from the project's official documentation, because text similarity cannot judge repository-level docs.

findings.basis: Web search summaries: arXiv 2603.21178 (340 repositories, 4,137 views; 'granularity mismatches'); arXiv 2604.08293 CIAO ('incomplete or misleading diagrams'); arXiv 2607.26100 systematic review ('hallucinated elements, incorrect relationships … violations of metamodel constraints'); arXiv 2510.24428 CodeWikiBench rubric method. Only the summaries were read.

findings.claim: Model-based architecture tools (Structurizr for C4) keep views consistent by construction: one model of elements and relationships, and every diagram a view derived from it. Names, descriptions and relationships therefore cannot drift between zoom levels, whereas drawing tools copy elements and drift. C4 also says to draw only the levels that add value; context and container usually suffice.

moves.title: One system model, many views (the Structurizr pattern), replacing per-diagram node lists
moves.what: The draft gains one `model`: elements {id, label, type: person|system|external|container|component|store|queue|file|other, parent?, citations | derived ref} and relationships {id, from, to, label, citations | derived ref}, each a claim exactly as diagram elements are today. Structural figure kinds (containment, graph, the hero) become views: {id, question, scope: elementId|root, level: context|container|component, include?: [ids], exclude?: [ids], layoutHint?}. The renderer computes each view: the elements at that level inside the scope, plus external neighbours. Implied relationships are computed too: if component A in container X relates to Y, the container view shows X→Y, rendered as 'implied by A→Y' in its text alternative and evidence pop. Sequence, swimlane and state figures reference model elements as their participants or lanes by id. Zoom links (I2-M2) fall out for free, because a view's scope element is clickable in its parent view. The I2-M2 refinement check becomes unnecessary: consistency holds by construction.
moves.why: This adopts the one idea that makes hand-made architecture documentation coherent across pages and removes a class of LLM error (the same component named three ways in three figures, I5-F4). It also makes the model the scaffold derived structure feeds: I1-M3's derived units become model elements with derived refs, and the author adds runtime relationships and groupings on top.
moves.truth_preservation: Each model element and relationship is checked once, not per figure. Implied relationships are mechanically derived from cited ones and say so: they are never drawn as if a source stated the container-level edge directly, which would be a VIS-7 violation. Their provenance attribute is 'computed from relationships'.
moves.generalization: C4's levels are generic, and other shapes map onto them (I2-M2). Element types are a closed, small set, with 'other' as an escape and a label.

moves.title: Three canonical viewpoints per system: building blocks, runtime, deployment (arc42 / 4+1)
moves.what: The page plan's architecture content is organised around three viewpoints, each a view kind on the shared model (I5-M1). Building blocks: containment views at context and container levels. Runtime: sequence or swimlane views of the one to three most important scenarios, which double as the running example's steps (I4-M3). Deployment: where things run, derived wherever the repository declares it (Dockerfile, compose, Kubernetes, Terraform, systemd units: I1-M1 T1), otherwise Unknown or from docs. A viewpoint the evidence cannot fill gets an `unresolved` disposition (a library has no deployment view, and says so in one line). arc42's 'crosscutting concepts' and 'risks and technical debt' become question-pack entries (I3-M2), answered only when the sources state them.
moves.why: It replaces the four fixed owner topics' implicit architecture coverage with a well-tested, project-neutral checklist of the views a reader needs. The deployment view in particular is often fully derivable, and no current Redis figure shows it.
moves.truth_preservation: Viewpoints are slots with honest dispositions. A derived deployment view is Observed (I1-M2), and a docs-sourced one is cited Inferred.
moves.generalization: 4+1 and arc42 were built to be domain-neutral. Shape packs choose which runtime scenarios to show (request, invocation, build, deploy, training run).

derive-rules (compose, Kubernetes, Terraform, Dockerfile) feeding the deployment view

moves.title: Granularity discipline: a view's level constrains what its elements may be
moves.what: The fix for the most-reported defect of auto-generated architecture views (I5-F2) is to make a view's `level` constrain its elements mechanically. At context level an element must be a person, system or external. At container level it must be a unit, service, store or queue: a derived manifest unit, a deployable or a data store, never a function. At component level it may be a module, package or file. `check` advises when an element at container level has citations that are all single spans inside one function-sized range (under about 40 lines in one source file), or a label in code-symbol form (reusing RS-13's identifier detector). It suggests moving the element to a component view or a deep dive.
moves.why: Granularity mismatch makes architecture figures unreadable: a 'system overview' with `processCommand` next to 'Replica'. The Redis workflow figure mixes levels this way ('Run command' beside 'Feed replicas').
moves.truth_preservation: Advisory only. It shapes the picture and asserts nothing.
moves.generalization: Level semantics are project-neutral. The 'unit' notion comes from derived manifests where they exist and from directories otherwise.
integration_points: check-derive.ts: citation-span-size heuristic per model element
slices: S1: the label-shape and span-size advisories per view level.

moves.title: Harvest the project's own decision records and docs IA before writing any
moves.what: Two recognizers, both data-only shape-pack entries (I3-M2). (a) ADR harvest: docs/adr, doc/adr, docs/decisions, architecture/decisions, and the MADR, Nygard or log4brains layouts, recognised by path plus a heading pattern (Status, Context, Decision, Consequences). Each becomes a decision card whose fields are verified quotations or derived rows, Observed, rendered in P8's 'Choices and costs' index, and attributed to the maintainers by its path. The author writes only the bridge prose linking a decision to the mechanism it shaped. (b) Diátaxis-aware routing: the docs-site nav (I3-M1) is classified into tutorial, how-to, reference and explanation by nav labels and paths (deterministic keyword rules, Unknown otherwise). The dossier stays in explanation mode and links out to the project's own tutorials and how-tos as 'In the project's own docs' route cards, naming paths at the pinned revision, so it never re-writes a tutorial.
moves.why: The best evidence of why a design is what it is is a maintainer's own decision record, and the current schema makes the agent paraphrase it. Diátaxis's central lesson (do not mix explanation with tutorial or reference) maps onto keeping the manifesto short (L4) while routing readers to depth the project already wrote.
moves.truth_preservation: Decision fields are quotations or derived rows, so they are Observed with exact spans. The classification of the docs IA is a deterministic keyword rule with Unknown as fallback. Route cards name in-tree paths only (no egress).
moves.generalization: ADRs are common in mature service and infrastructure repos and absent in most small ones. Absence costs nothing: the recognizer simply yields nothing, and P8's authored cards remain.

moves.title: Make the differentiator visible: a per-figure and per-page evidence tally

units.framing: Run 3 found the integrity core world-class and the product built around it unproven. Its moves, P3/P5/P8 (argument), P9/P10 (breadth) and P12 (visuals), all ask the authoring agent to do more and better. This run's central idea is different: Syzygy should observe more, so the agent writes less and draws almost nothing from scratch. A deterministic structure record of the pinned tree, labelled Observed under doctrine as written (trust-and-evidence.md:105 plus RFC7-28's computed visuals; only a dossier spec clause stands in the way), becomes four things. It is the scaffold for the system model and its views. It is the witness that confirms or challenges every arrow. It is the denominator for coverage. It is the trait profile that makes the page plan general. On top of that sit one system model with many views, figures that explain and link without script, and instruments that measure figures and reading depths exactly instead of by judgement. Every external or generality claim here is Inferred: all six live runs are of redis/redis.

ranked.title: Verified relationships: typed arrows that derived structure confirms or challenges, a generated legend, and a per-figure evidence tally
ranked.what: Every edge gets a closed `relation` type. For derivable types (imports, depends-on, contains, deploys-to), `check` upgrades an edge to derived and Observed when the structure record witnesses it. It raises a finding when derive's coverage of those files was complete and no witness exists. An edge whose citations touch neither endpoint's files gets an advisory. Each figure's legend is generated from the encodings it actually uses. Each figure and page shows a computed tally ('14 relationships: 9 derived by Syzygy · 5 cited readings · 0 unsupported').
ranked.truth_preservation: Deterministic evidence may establish an element; missing evidence only challenges, and only under complete coverage. The tally is computed, and its vocabulary is the legend's (VIS-7).
ranked.generalization: Relation types and locality checks are project-neutral. Witnesses exist wherever format or lexical rules cover the ecosystem; elsewhere the check stays silent.

ranked.title: Pinned-tree structure record and trait profile: Syzygy derives the repository's shape before anyone writes
ranked.what: A deterministic `derive` stage writes derived/structure.json. It holds T0 path-only tree facts (sizes, language mix, vendored and generated code excluded by linguist rules and .gitattributes), T1 format recognizers (workspace and package manifests, binaries and scripts, CI jobs and needs, compose, Kubernetes and Terraform topology), and later T2 lexical import graphs. Each fact carries {rule, version, path, lines}, and every rule carries its own coverage. A trait vector (has-cli, has-library-api, has-service, has-plugins, has-infrastructure, has-pipeline, has-firmware, has-data-model, docs-site nav, licence by SPDX match, size class) is computed with witness paths. The record is delivered the way census.ts delivers its census, or named by the brief after a REQ-034 spec amendment.
ranked.truth_preservation: Claims stay at the rule's own resolution ('declares a dependency', never 'calls at runtime'). Output is byte-identical on re-run and re-checked by digest. An unparsed or withheld input is Unknown, never 'no edges'.
ranked.generalization: It keys on file formats, never on projects or archetypes. A repository with no recognised format still gets T0 and an honest Unknown remainder.

ranked.title: Figures that explain and link, with no script: diagram-first walks, cross-highlighting and click-to-source
ranked.what: A section may declare a `walk`: ordered steps, each binding a cited block to figure elements. Numbered badges appear on the walked elements. Clicking a step highlights its element via `:target`, and hovering or focusing does so via a generated per-figure `:has()` rule; inline style is already CSP-allowed. An HTML hit layer over the inert SVG makes every node and edge label a link to its first citation's line anchor (fnry.20), with a native popover when it has several citations. `check` requires every element of a walked figure to be walked or listed as self-evident, and advises on steps that only restate a label or cite evidence disjoint from their element. The walk becomes the figure's text alternative.
ranked.truth_preservation: Walk blocks are claims under every existing rule. Links are computed from checked citations. The SVG allowlist does not change.
ranked.generalization: Works for every figure kind with addressable elements.

ranked.what: A block's tree level is its depth: 30 seconds, 5 minutes, or everything. A CSS-only switch shows one depth at a time, and an Unknown that qualifies a parent is promoted to the parent's depth. `check` reports words and reading time per depth. The P7 probe runs per depth: depth 1 must yield purpose, beneficiary and thesis, and depth 2 all seven frozen answers. Glossary terms gain `homeBlock`, `aliases` and `dependsOn`. The renderer's existing surface-form matcher runs over the reading order and advises when a term is used before its home block or definitions form a cycle. The glossary renders in topological order. Each page type gets a fixed composition the renderer owns: answer, figure, walk, cost, then 'Go deeper' and 'Related', both computed.
ranked.truth_preservation: Hiding is presentation only, and the promotion rule keeps material qualifications at the depth of the claim they qualify. Term bindings are presentation. 'Related' links are labelled 'shares terms with', never a dependency.
ranked.generalization: Depth comes from the tree, terms from the project's own vocabulary, page types are generic. Budgets scale with R9's size tier.

The model is seeded from derived units (R6) where they exist.

first_three.why: If only three could ship, these three change what a reader of any repository sees, and each makes the next one cheaper. R2, the structure record and trait profile, is the substrate. Slice 1 is path-only, reads no blob, and doubles as the cheapest generality measurement available before any non-Redis live run. With R10's one-clause spec change (rank 10, cost 1, which should ride along), it gives the first solid, Observed boxes any dossier has had. R5, one model with many views, is the visual transformation the owner asked for: one hero picture of the system on the landing, zoom into regions, and consistency across pages by construction, seeded from R2's units. R3, walks with click-to-source, makes every figure explain itself and link to evidence with no script. It is also the cheapest high-value move (cost 2), and it fixes how figures read today. R1 ranks higher on truth-per-cost and should follow immediately: its slice 1 needs nothing from these three.

objections.objection: Building generality machinery before any non-Redis run repeats the risk run 3's strategy reviewer raised: the owner question 'run the current pipeline on two or three non-Redis repositories before building P9, P10 or P12' is still open. Format recognizers are a long tail that could grow into a code-intelligence product. T1 rules read blobs, so screening and consented content classes apply, and a withheld manifest silently thins the record. A rich derived record also pulls the dossier toward the catalogue L7 warns against.
objections.response: Slice 1 is path-only, and it is itself the cheapest generality measurement (it runs on any repo in seconds with no LLM, R13 tier A). Recognizers are capped at three structured formats plus line-oriented files, with T3 explicitly deferred. Withheld inputs show as Unknown remainders, not silence. The catalogue lives on reference and map pages, one step from the argument, never in it.

objections.objection: It is a schema v5 migration that forces an LLM to commit to one coherent model up front. That may lower draft quality and raise repair cycles, already the dominant cost (18 of 23 fidelity verdicts not ready across five runs). C4's levels fit servers better than libraries or docs-only repos. A rendered model also invites readers to take it as the complete architecture.
objections.response: Seed the model from R2's derived units so most elements arrive pre-checked. Allow one-level models. Render coverage ('model covers 9 of 31 units; full map') on every view. Ship slice 1 (a hero on today's schema) first to measure whether one picture helps before migrating.

objections.objection: Binding prose to figure elements can make writing stilted ('Step 1… Step 2…'), and walk coverage invites gaming with trivial steps for every element. Per-element `:has()` CSS rules grow page CSS linearly with figure size, and `:has()` hover cross-highlighting is invisible to touch users.
objections.response: Walks are opt-in per section, `selfEvident` absorbs trivial elements, and the restatement advisory flags padding. CSS rules are generated only for walked elements, bounded by the 40-node schema cap. Touch users get `:target` on tap, which is the primary path. Hover is enhancement.

pictures.small_rust_cli: [Inferred: no non-Redis run exists] A reader opening the dossier for a short Rust command-line search tool sees the title, a one-sentence thesis quoted from its README, and a small hero figure. In it the shell, stdin and the filesystem surround the binary, whose three workspace crates are solid boxes derived from Cargo.toml (Observed, each a link to its manifest lines). The caption tally reads '5 relationships: 3 derived by Syzygy · 2 cited readings'. A depth switch offers the 30-second view (thesis, hero, three one-line Pole answers) or the 5-minute view. A ribbon says 'Following: rg -i todo src/, taken from tests/feature.rs'. 'How a search runs' is a four-lane swimlane (argument parsing, directory walker, searcher, printer) that collapses to a stepper on a phone. Its four numbered prose steps light up their lanes on tap and open the exact source lines on click. One deep dive covers the matcher, with a record figure of its configuration. Reference pages hold the computed crate graph, the CI pipeline map from the workflow files, and the release timeline from tags. The glossary reads top to bottom as a primer. The whole dossier is perhaps six pages, because the profile put it in size class S and the tier said read everything.
pictures.ts_monorepo_300_packages: [Inferred] For a 300-package TypeScript monorepo, the profile reports a workspace of 300 units across apps/ and packages/, size class L, has-service plus has-library-api plus has-cli, with vendored and generated code excluded. The landing hero is a container view grouped into nine domains derived from directory and workspace structure, with the chip 'showing 9 groups of 300 packages · full map'. Each group zooms into a component view of its packages, whose dependency arrows are derived from package.json and solid, plus a few dashed runtime arrows ('web app sends GraphQL requests to api') that the author cited from code. The coverage map says what was read: deep prose for the 14 most central packages, derived-only cards for 283 more (name, path, size, dependents: all Observed), and 3 withheld by screening, denominated in first-party bytes. An atlas page shows the 300 packages as small multiples per domain. The deployment viewpoint is derived from compose and Kubernetes files. The build pipeline is derived from the workspace task config and CI workflows. The running example follows one request from an end-to-end test through four domains. 'Choices and costs' leads with the repo's own ADRs as Observed cards. Every figure prints its tally, and a figure whose pixels a fresh reader could not transcribe at phone width has been split before the owner ever sees it.

units.framing: A great technical manifesto has a small visual language, used consistently: one hero picture of the whole system, zoomable regions, flows drawn as lanes over time, states as cycles, data as laid-out records, history as a line, and choices as a matrix. Each figure answers one question and is walked by the prose beside it. Today the schema has six diagram kind names over one flat node/edge list and one layered left-to-right layout. Nodes cannot contain nodes, nothing in a figure is clickable, and nothing binds a prose step to the element it explains. Run 3's P12 listed the missing kinds. This lens gives each kind a checkable schema shape and a layout, makes the split between SVG figures and HTML figures explicit, and adds three mechanisms P12 lacks: zoom levels with a refinement check, diagram-first 'walks' with script-free cross-highlighting, and click-to-source on every element.

moves.title: Typed figure kinds: one schema shape and one layout per question, HTML where HTML wins
moves.what: Replace the single `diagrams[]` shape with a discriminated union, keeping today's form as kind `graph`. Each kind's schema carries only what its layout needs, so a malformed figure is a schema error, not an ugly render. The kinds: (1) `sequence`: participants (2 to 6, each a node with citations); messages in order, each {from, to, label, citations, returns?}; optional frames {kind: loop|alt|opt, label, fromMsg, toMsg}. Layout is a fixed grid (participant columns, message rows), drawn as SVG; there is nothing to optimise. (2) `swimlane`: lanes (actors or components) and steps {lane, label, citations, after?: [stepIds]}. Layout is a grid of lane rows by topological-rank columns, drawn as SVG. At 390 px it switches to a vertical stepper (HTML <ol>) with a lane chip on each step. This is the replacement for long `flow` chains. (3) `containment`: nodes with `parent`, giving a compound graph. Layout is recursive: lay out each group's children, size the group box, then lay out groups. Hierarchy depth is at most 3. (4) `state`: states, an initial state, transitions {from, to, event, guard?}; laid out with the existing layered engine with back edges, plus self-loops as arcs. (5) `record`: fields {name, type?, size?, offset?, note, citations}; HTML flex strip, wrapping. (6) `stack`: ordered layers, each with items; HTML grid. (7) `timeline`: ordered events {when, label, citations}, where `when` is a version or a date as the source states it; HTML <ol> on an axis. (8) `matrix`: rows by columns with cell values from a closed set {yes, no, partial, unknown, text}; HTML table with a legend. Every kind keeps per-element `epistemic`, citations or a `derived` ref (I1-M2), and a mandatory `question` field (the reader question it answers).
moves.why: The owner asked for flowcharts, architectures and diagrams that are beautiful. A layout specialised to its kind is the difference between a figure and a box chain. P12 named the kinds but no shapes or layouts. Making the schema per kind is what lets an LLM produce good figures reliably: the schema forbids the shapes that make bad ones.
moves.truth_preservation: Unchanged at its core: every node, edge, message, step, field, cell and event is a claim with citations, a derived ref, or Unknown. New: a frame (loop or alt) is a claim and needs citations. Adjacency in an HTML kind (row order in a stack, position on a timeline) is declared meaning, so `stack` and `timeline` order must be cited or derived, never a layout accident. The legend is generated per kind from what that figure actually uses (VIS-7: no legend entry without a population, no encoding without a legend entry).
moves.generalization: The kinds are project-neutral question types (who talks to whom over time, what contains what, what states exist, how bytes are laid out, what changed when, how options compare). Archetypes (lens 3) only change which kinds a page plan prefers.

moves.title: Zoomable system map: a hero context figure, container and component zooms, and a refinement check
moves.what: Add C4-style zoom levels as first-class structure. The landing page requires one hero `containment` figure at `zoom: context` (the system, its users, the external systems it talks to) or at `zoom: container` for a single deployable. Any node may carry `zoomTo: <diagramId>`. The target diagram declares `zoomOf: <nodeId>`, and its boundary box is that node. The page renders a zoom glyph on the node, and clicking it lands on the child figure's page. `check` enforces refinement consistency mechanically: every edge in the parent that touches the zoomed node X, say X→Y, must appear in the child as an edge from some node inside X's boundary to Y, which the child shows as an external stub. The child may not invent an external neighbour the parent lacks, unless that neighbour is added to the parent too. The hero figure's regions also carry `pole` links, so the landing picture doubles as the navigation map (the Pole list becomes a picture of the system).
moves.why: It is the one picture a newcomer needs first (RS-8, 'the opening'), and it makes depth navigable spatially, not only through a sidebar. The refinement check is something no hand-made or auto-wiki architecture site does: it guarantees that zooming in never contradicts the zoomed-out picture.
moves.truth_preservation: Refinement consistency is a mechanical, deterministic check on the draft's own graph, with no LLM in it. Each level's elements keep their own citations. Where the derived structure (I1-M1) exists, the container level should start from the derived unit or service graph (I1-M3 `base`), so the hero's boxes are Observed. A context-level external actor ('users', 'operators') is a claim and needs a citation or an Unknown mark.
moves.generalization: Context → container → component applies to libraries (context: the host application; containers: the public modules), CLIs (context: shell, filesystem, network; containers: subcommands), servers, monorepos (containers: packages, with the derived unit graph as the base) and IaC (containers: environments and modules). A repo too small for three levels uses one level; the check only binds levels that exist.

moves.title: Diagram-first walks: prose is bound to the figure elements it explains, with script-free cross-highlighting
moves.what: A section may open with a figure and declare its prose as a `walk`: an ordered list of steps, each {elements: [nodeIds/edgeIds], block}. The renderer puts a numbered badge on each walked element and the same number on the prose step. Cross-highlighting needs no script. Each prose step is `<a href="#fig3-e4">`, and the figure's elements carry ids, so `:target` highlights the element on click. A per-figure generated `<style>` rule such as `figure:has(.walk li[data-el=e4]:is(:hover,:focus-within)) [data-el=e4] { stroke-width:3 }` highlights on hover and focus, which works in evergreen browsers with no JS. `check` enforces: every walked id exists; every element of a walked figure is walked or listed in `selfEvident` (anti-decoration: a figure nobody explains is a finding); no step merely restates its element's label (a lexical check: step text minus stopwords ⊄ element label, advisory). The text alternative for the figure is the walk itself, in order. That is the cited claim list RFC7-34 asks for, read as a story rather than a flat list of nodes and edges.
moves.why: It answers 'diagrams lead, prose follows' (readability rule 2) mechanically rather than by exhortation, and kills the RS-20 failure of prose retelling the diagram edge by edge. It gives the most-loved feature of high-end explorable explanations (step sync) at zero CSP cost, which P12's progressive-enhancement script does not need for this case.
moves.truth_preservation: A step's block is a claim under every existing rule. Binding adds a checkable relation: the block's citations should overlap the walked element's citations or derived source (advisory finding when disjoint, catching prose that explains an edge with unrelated evidence).
moves.generalization: Any figure kind with addressable elements, so all of I2-M1's kinds.

moves.title: Figure policy by page type, and three rules that stop decorative diagrams
moves.what: A small table, which is data rather than prose, maps page type to required figure kinds, each satisfiable by a produced figure or an `omitted` disposition with a reason. Landing: one hero context or container figure (I2-M2). Workflow section: one `sequence` or `swimlane` per end-to-end workflow. Mechanism deep dive: one figure of any graph kind or `record`. Choices index (P8): one `matrix` where two or more alternatives are named by the sources. Reference: derived maps (I1-M3, I1-M4). Anti-decoration rules, each a `check` advisory or finding. (1) Information floor: a graph with fewer than 3 nodes, or a linear chain of 3 or fewer, is flagged ('this is a sentence, write it'). (2) Every figure states its `question`, and the comprehension probe (P7) asks that question with only the figure and its caption visible. A figure the reader cannot answer from is a design finding. (3) Walk coverage (I2-M3): an unexplained figure is a finding. Plus duplicate detection: two figures with a Jaccard node-label overlap of at least 0.8 on one page are flagged.
moves.why: P12 said 'spec amendment for required diagrams' without saying which or how to stop quota-filling. AUTHORING.md says 'without a quota' and 'a missing drawable one is a blocking finding', and only the design reviewer enforces it today. A table plus three mechanical rules moves most of that from judgement to check.
moves.truth_preservation: Requirements are always satisfiable honestly: `omitted` and `unresolved` dispositions with a reason exist already (draft-schema.ts:108-112), so a figure is never forced where evidence is missing (VIS-2, AUTHORING 'Do not manufacture internals').
moves.generalization: Page types are project-neutral. Archetype packs (lens 3) can add rows, for example a CLI's command-surface page requiring a `matrix` of subcommands by flags.

units.framing: A figure can fail in two independent ways. It can be untrue: an element or relationship the sources do not support, or an encoding that implies meaning the data lacks. It can be unreadable: crossings, overlaps, text too small, too wide, or a picture that does not answer its question. Today the schema guarantees one thing mechanically (every node and edge carries at least one citation, and endpoints resolve). The fidelity review judges support in prose, and the design reviewer reads HTML without pixels. Run 3's P6 adds page screenshots and overflow asserts, and P7 adds a page-level comprehension probe. This lens adds four sharper instruments. Typed relationships that derived structure can confirm or challenge. Pure-geometry layout lints computed at render, with no browser. A pixel round-trip test that grades legibility exactly against the figure's own model, with no LLM judge in the grading. A figure zoo that pins each layout kind.

findings.claim: Mechanically guaranteed today: every diagram node and edge cites at least one span (`citations(1)`), and an edge's endpoints are nodes of its diagram. Not guaranteed: that an edge's citation concerns either endpoint, that a node names something that exists at the pinned revision, that an edge's meaning is typed (AUTHORING.md asks for 'typed edges' and 'edge meaning', but the schema has only a free `label`), or that the legend's entries have any population.
