moves.title: Typed relationships, with derived structure that can confirm or challenge them
moves.what: Every edge or relationship gets `relation`, a closed set: imports, depends-on, contains, calls, sends-to, reads, writes, spawns, configures, deploys-to, triggers, transitions-to, other(label). Three mechanical checks follow. (1) Endpoint-evidence locality: each edge's citations should fall in a file belonging to either endpoint (endpoint files come from the element's own citations or its derived unit), or in a documentation file. An edge whose evidence touches neither endpoint gets an advisory, a cheap pre-filter for the 'hallucinated relationship' class the literature reports (I5-F2). (2) Derived witness for derivable relations: for imports, depends-on, contains and deploys-to between elements with derived identity, where derive covered those files, `check` looks for a witness in derived/structure.json. If it finds one, the edge is upgraded to derived (solid, Observed, I1-M2). If coverage was complete and it finds none, that is a finding: 'derived structure shows no import between these units; cite the relation or change its type'. Where coverage was incomplete, the edge stays Inferred and the check is silent. (3) Legend population: the legend is generated per figure from the encodings actually used, so no legend entry has an empty population and no encoding lacks an entry (VIS-7, I2-F4).
moves.why: This puts the strongest truth instrument Polaris has (deterministic re-derivation) onto the most error-prone visual claim (the arrow). The fidelity reviewer then spends attention on runtime relations (calls, sends-to), which nothing can derive, instead of on facts a parser can settle.
moves.truth_preservation: It follows doctrine's seam in reverse and safely: deterministic evidence may establish (upgrade to Observed), while missing derived evidence only challenges, as a finding that asks for a citation or a type change, and only where derive's coverage of those files was complete. Otherwise silence (VIS-2: incomplete coverage proves nothing). The relation type is a claim and is checked like the label.
moves.generalization: Relation types are project-neutral. Derived witnesses exist wherever T1 or T2 rules cover the ecosystem, and checks (1) and (3) work everywhere.

moves.title: Geometry lints at render time: measure every figure before any browser runs
moves.what: The layout functions already compute every box, curve and label. A pure `lintFigure(layout, targets)` reports, per figure and per target width (390, 768 and 1,440, at the column width the template gives each): effective minimum text size after fit-to-width scaling; whether it must scroll; edge crossings (segment-pair intersection over the sampled curves the layout already makes for leader placement); label-label and label-node overlaps; aspect ratio; node count against a per-kind readable bound; longest unwrapped label. Rules: if the fit-to-width text drops below 12 px at a target, the renderer must choose the kind's narrow variant (stepper for a swimlane, top-to-bottom for a graph, split for an oversized view), or else emit a design finding. Crossings above a kind-specific threshold produce an advisory naming the edges and suggesting a split view or grouping. Every lint result is stored in size-report.json and shown on the review report. The hard-coded width rule (I6-F2) is retired in favour of the selected variant.
moves.why: It sharpens P6. Headless Chrome screenshots are the truth for pixels, but they are slow, need a browser, and run after the fact. Most figure failures (I2-F2, I6-F2) are determined by geometry the renderer already has. A pure lint runs in the unit tier and in `check`'s preview, and lets the renderer adapt instead of only reporting.
moves.truth_preservation: Lints are measurements of presentation, deterministic and stored, never claims about the project. A failed lint never hides an element. It changes the variant or raises a finding.
moves.generalization: Kind-generic geometry. Thresholds are per kind, not per project.
integration_points: a new apps/three-surface-poc/src/polaris-generation/figure-lint.ts (pure, using diagram-layout.ts outputs: curveSamples, placeEdgeLabels boxes)

moves.title: Pixel round-trip: a fresh vision reader transcribes the rendered figure, graded exactly against its model
moves.what: For each figure, render a screenshot at 390 px and at 1,440 px (P6's cdp-browser). Hand only the PNG and the caption to a fresh reader session (vision-capable, no draft, no HTML). Ask it to transcribe the figure as JSON: elements, relationships with labels and direction, groupings. Grade mechanically against the figure's own model as set comparisons after label normalisation: element recall and precision, relationship recall and precision, direction accuracy, grouping agreement. No LLM judges the answer. Add 2 to 3 template questions generated from the model itself ('What does Read query hand to Parse command?', answer: the edge label; 'Which elements does redis-server talk to?', answer: the neighbour set), also graded exactly. Store per-figure legibility scores, run over run. A score under a threshold (relationship recall below 0.9 at 1,440 px, for example) is a design finding naming the figure and the misread elements.
moves.why: It answers 'how would anyone know a diagram is good?' with an objective, cheap and repeatable number: if a careful reader cannot recover the figure's own relationships from its pixels, the figure fails at its one job, whatever the layout aesthetics. It sharpens P6 (pixels) and P7 (comprehension) into a figure-level instrument with exact grading, which avoids the self-consistency trap run 3's P7 correction names.
moves.truth_preservation: It measures legibility, not truth: the answer key is the checked model, whose truth the fidelity review and derivation establish separately. Scores are advice stored with the session identity and model, and never feed a label. The reader session gets no source text, so it cannot leak evidence into its reading.
moves.generalization: Kind- and project-neutral. Template questions come from the model's structure.

moves.title: Figure zoo: adversarial golden fixtures per kind plus metric-diff re-render of every stored draft
moves.what: For each figure kind (I2-M1), a fixed set of adversarial models: long labels (60 characters, CJK, unbroken identifiers), fan-out of 12, a chain of 15, a chain ending in a fan-out (the Redis case), cycles and self-loops, containment three deep, 40 nodes, empty optional fields. Each fixture asserts geometry lints (I6-M2) as literal expected values and stores a golden SVG. A re-render script renders every stored real draft on disk (the six Redis runs' drafts) after any layout change and diffs lint metrics per figure, not bytes. It reports improvements and regressions by figure id, and a regression in effective text size or crossings fails the change.
moves.why: It sharpens P6's 'render-regression script' with the right comparison (metrics, not bytes, which change on every improvement) and pins the layout kinds the way conformance fixtures pin the core. Without it, each new kind risks the band-wrap gap the Redis flow fell into (I2-F2).
moves.truth_preservation: Fixtures are inputs with literal expected values (the repository's conformance discipline). Real drafts are read-only inputs.
moves.generalization: The zoo is kind-indexed. Shape-matrix fixtures (I3-M5) add realistic sizes per repository shape.
integration_points: a new scripts/polaris_figure_rerender.mjs over the state directory's drafts (read-only)
